content.title: The duration of tasks AI completes autonomously doubles about every four months
content.content:
Why now ① Rise of foundation models and AI progress
The length of tasks AI can complete autonomously doubles about every four months.
METR, a US research organization measuring AI capability, asks how many hours of human work AI can complete with 50% success.
Source: METR, “Time Horizon 1.1”, January 2026. The Opus 4.6 value reflects the March 2026 calculation correction, which reduced recent models' values by up to 20%. METR stopped updates in September 2026.
50% time horizon — task duration completed with 50% success:
Model | Release date | Duration
GPT-4 | March 2023 | 3.5 minutes
Claude 3.7 Sonnet | February 2025 | 1 hour
o3 | April 2025 | 2 hours
GPT-5 | August 2025 | 3.6 hours
Claude Opus 4.5 | November 2025 | 5.3 hours
Claude Opus 4.6 | February 2026 | 12 hours
About 200 times in three years: from GPT-4's 3.5 minutes to Claude Opus 4.6's 12 hours. Since 2023, the duration has doubled about every four months.
At 80% reliability, it shrinks to just over one hour.

Displayed answer: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a method in which relevant documents or information are retrieved and a language model generates a response based on that information. It is used to improve the quality and relevance of generated text by incorporating external knowledge. RAG can be applied in various contexts, including text, images and video, and is a versatile tool for generating accurate outputs appropriate to the context. The process usually involves searching for relevant documents, combining them with the input query, and then using a language model to generate a response. This approach is particularly useful for complex queries that require external knowledge beyond the language model's training data. RAG is considered a way to enhance a language model's capabilities by accessing and using external databases and knowledge sources. [0]

content.title: Probably not sufficient: reasons 1 and 2
content.content:
Thinking Through an Example
Probably not. Why...
Reasons 1 & 2
Source: Google, “Rules of Machine Learning: Best Practices for ML Engineering,” Rule #23
Reason 1: Averages hide things. Production data
differs from development data
• What if accuracy varies greatly by question type?
• You, the developer, are not an average user (Rule #23 “You
are not a typical end user.”)
• Production brings surprises (write “No course-admin questions” and
they still come)
• Models always degrade (models have a shelf life too)
Reason 2: Requirements beyond functionality,
such as speed and cost (non-functional requirements)
• What response speed is needed?
• Is batch processing OK? Or must each question be answered immediately?
• What user environment can we assume?

content.title: Today: inside [3] Model training — the foundation model itself
content.content:
Recap of the previous lecture

Recall: what are the five stages of AI engineering? Which one do we cover today? The answer is in the diagram below.
Problem formulation: define inputs and outputs; define the evaluation method; estimate feasibility and value. Lecture 4.
Data collection: prepare training and evaluation data; design the data flow. Lecture 5.
Model training: select and adapt models; isolate the causes of failure. Lectures 2, 3 and 6.
Deployment: release in a usable form; system architecture and load handling. Lecture 7.
Improvement: monitor operations; automated testing and rollout; MLOps. Lectures 8–10.
The previous lecture's example was a chatbot that answers questions during lectures. We will use it again today.

content.title: Build a chatbot and you soon encounter these difficulties
content.content:
Today's question
Build a chatbot and you soon encounter these difficulties.
They are not accidents: they follow from how foundation models work.
The same question gets a different answer each time: ask “What is RAG?” five times and receive five different answers.
It confidently says something wrong: it plausibly describes a nonexistent “Lecture 14 assignment”.
Given long documents, it misses the middle: even with all the lecture materials, it cannot answer about slides in the middle.
Today's goal: explain a model's limits from its mechanisms, choose between “provide information/select a model”, “adapt it”, and “let it think more” according to the problem, and measure the effects.

content.title: Today's four questions — 15 minutes each
content.content:
Today's outline
Today's four questions — 15 minutes each
1. Why do answers vary and contain errors? LLMs select the next words probabilistically.
2. Where should we intervene to make a model more capable? According to the problem: provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more.
3. What models exist, and how do we choose? A map of language, images, audio, time series and more. The deciding factors are our own evaluation and “cost < benefit”.
4. When and how should we adapt the model we choose? Fine-Tuning is good at changing behavior and less effective at adding knowledge. Try it in the exercise.

content.title: Today's topic is the model itself
content.content:
Today's outline
Today's topic is the “model” itself.
ChatGPT and Claude apps are systems with tools such as search, code execution and memory around the model. We cover that outer layer in Lecture 3.
Service, such as a ChatGPT or Claude app = system.
Outer elements: search; code execution; memory and files; long instructions.
Model (LLM): today's focus.
The outer layer — agents that operate using tools — is covered in Lecture 3.
Even with that outer layer, today's properties remain:
• Answering about current information through search automates providing documents (RAG). It does not add to the model's knowledge.
• Answers vary even when search results are supplied. Misreading and incorrect source attribution can also occur.
• Too many results can cause information in the middle to be missed and increase cost.
The preparatory homework and exercises use a “raw model” without this outer layer. You can experience the difference.

content.title: Six terms to know first
content.content:
Today's outline
Six terms to know first
Details follow in each part. Here are brief meanings; return to this slide if unsure.
Token: a unit into which text is split; the unit for counting length and cost. Part 1.
Parameter (weight): a number inside the model. There are billions to trillions, adjusted during training. Part 1.
Pre-training: learning next-token prediction from large amounts of text; the foundation of knowledge. Part 2.
Post-training: learning how to answer from examples and evaluation. Part 2.
Inference-time compute: increasing the amount of thinking when answering. Part 2.
Fine-Tuning (FT): doing post-training ourselves on a small scale. Part 4.
Lecture 1 review: RAG retrieves documents relevant to the question and puts them into the input before the model answers. Details in Lecture 5.

content.section: LLMs select the next words probabilistically

content.title: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
content.content:
Lecture 2 — Part 1/4, approximately 15 minutes
LLMs select the next words probabilistically.
Why do chatbot answers vary, and why can they be confidently wrong?

content.title: An LLM keeps selecting the next token probabilistically
content.content:
1/4: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
An LLM is a machine that keeps selecting the “next token” probabilistically.
The core of these 15 minutes: an LLM calculates probabilities for the next token and selects one. This causes both variation in answers and plausible errors.
Token: a unit into which text is split. Both length and cost are counted in tokens.
Because selection is probabilistic (sampling), answers can differ even for the same question.
Pre-training learns what is plausible. Post-training moves the model toward correctness, but does not guarantee it. We therefore need to measure its behavior and work with these properties.

content.title: Tokenization: splitting text into units the model handles
content.content:
1/4: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
Tokenization: splitting text into units the model handles
Words, word fragments and symbols can be tokens. Model input/output length and cost are counted in tokens.
Example: split a student's question into tokens. The split differs by model; this diagram is illustrative.
The Japanese question means “What is RAG?”. Its illustrated token/ID pairs are:
“RAG” → 1000; “って” → 1037; “何” → 1074; “です” → 1111; “か” → 1148; “？” → 1185.
Each token becomes a number (ID), and the model receives a sequence of numbers.
Length limits are measured in tokens: the amount it can read at once, or context length, is also defined in tokens.
Cost is measured in tokens too: API charges depend on input and output token counts. See the cost estimate in the supplement.
Efficiency differs by language: the same content can require different token counts in different languages.

content.title: Calculate the next-token probabilities, select one, and repeat
content.content:
1/4: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
Calculate the “probabilities” of the next token, select one, and repeat.
A Transformer, the standard architecture of current LLMs, considers the whole context and outputs a probability distribution over the next token.
Source: the probabilities are illustrative values.
Input, or text so far:
Question: What is RAG?
Answer: RAG is a method that … documents relevant to the question.
Transformer → next-token probabilities:
“retrieves” 46%; “finds” 31%; “collects” 12%; “reads” 7%.
1. Select one according to its probability, for example “retrieves”.
2. Append the chosen token to the end of the input.
3. Calculate the next-token probabilities again.
4. Repeat until an “end” token appears.
What training teaches is a probability: “in this context, this is likely to come next”. The model itself has no built-in mechanism to directly verify factual correctness.

content.title: A model is a giant function with billions of numerical parameters
content.content:
1/4: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
A model is a giant function with billions of numbers, called parameters.
This is the same idea as coefficients in multiple regression. Training adjusts the numbers so predictions become accurate.
A familiar example: multiple regression.
Prediction = w₁ × area + w₂ × distance from the station + b.
Predicting rent: three coefficients, w₁, w₂ and b.
Next-token probability = f(tokens so far; w).
An LLM has billions to trillions of coefficients w.
Inside are many layers of additions and transformations: a neural network. Each connection has a coefficient.
Parameters (weights): these coefficients.
“7B” means 7 billion. At 16 bits, a 7B model's weights alone occupy about 14 GB. Ordinary FT also holds training state, requiring several times more memory.
Training = adjusting coefficients little by little so predictions approach the correct answers.
Pre-training, post-training and Fine-Tuning all adjust these coefficients. They differ in what data is used, which coefficients are changed, and by how much.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
Neural network diagram: input layer → hidden layer 1 → hidden layer 2 → output layer.

content.title: Sampling: how probabilities are used changes the character of answers
content.content:
1/4: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
Sampling: how we select from probabilities changes the character of answers.
Lower temperature produces more conservative answers; higher temperature produces more diversity. Even temperature 0 does not always make output completely constant.
Source: the probabilities are illustrative values.
Low temperature, for example 0.2:
“retrieves” 86%; “finds” 12%; “collects” 2%.
Almost always “retrieves”: stable but monotonous.
High temperature, for example 1.2:
“retrieves” 38%; “finds” 30%; “collects” 19%.
Selections are more spread out: more diversity, but also more misses.
This explains the variation you observed when changing temperature in the preparatory homework.
For a chatbot, use a lower setting for factual answers and a higher setting for brainstorming. Measure the effect to check.

content.title: Consequence 1: the same question can get a different answer each time
content.content:
1/4: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
Consequence 1: the same question can get a different answer each time.
Trying once and seeing it “work” is not an evaluation. Ask the same question multiple times and measure the variation too.
Illustrative example: ask “What is RAG?” five times. Legend: ✓ correct; ✗ wrong; ! insufficient.
1. A method that retrieves documents relevant to the question and builds an answer based on them.
2. A mechanism that retrieves external documents and adds them to the LLM's input before it answers.
3. A technique that generates text while supplementing knowledge through retrieval.
4. A method that further trains the model to memorize new knowledge.
5. A feature that summarizes and displays retrieved documents.
Three correct answers out of five.
• The first answer alone can look “perfect”, but it does not reveal the actual accuracy.
• Evaluate the same question multiple times. Look at the average and variation; see Lecture 4.
• Lowering temperature or providing reference documents can reduce variation.

content.title: Consequence 2: plausible answers even without knowledge
content.content:
1/4: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
Consequence 2: the model gives plausible answers even about things it does not know.
Because it probabilistically generates likely text, it can produce fluent errors, or hallucinations, on questions for which it lacks knowledge.
Illustrative example:
Student: When is the Lecture 14 assignment due?
Chatbot: The Lecture 14 assignment is “final presentation slides”, due Sunday, December 20 at 23:59.
In fact, Lecture 14 does not exist: there are 13 lectures. Even so, an answer that seems to fit the syllabus is generated.
Why this happens and how to handle it:
Mechanism: a plausible answer tends to receive a higher probability than “I don't know”.
Countermeasure — provide evidence: retrieve lecture materials and pass them in, using RAG in Lecture 5. Ask it to show its supporting sources too.
Countermeasure — measure: include unanswerable questions in the evaluation set and measure whether it can say “I don't know”.

content.title: Another limit: long contexts are not used evenly
content.content:
1/4: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
Another limit: long contexts are not used evenly.
Even when the amount a model can read at once increases, it can overlook information in the middle. Recent models show improvement, but evaluation for your own use case is still necessary.
Sources: N. F. Liu et al., “Lost in the Middle”, TACL 2024. For improvements and remaining challenges, see C.-P. Hsieh et al., “RULER”, COLM 2024, and related work.
Consider: what happens to accuracy when the answer is in the middle? Liu et al., Fig. 1.
Information in the middle is less likely to be used: a U-shaped curve. The dotted line is the case without supplied documents.
For a chatbot:
• Retrieve and provide only the portions related to the question, using RAG, rather than passing in all lecture materials together.
• Organize information in long conversations and documents using summaries or working notes.
• Vary the input length and measure whether accuracy decreases.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
Chart: 20 Total Retrieved Documents (~4K tokens).
Horizontal axis: Position of Document with the Answer. Vertical axis: Accuracy.
Legend: gpt-3.5-turbo-0613; gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 (closed-book).

content.title: Quiz 1: ready to release?
content.content:
Quiz 1/4
Quiz 1: ready to release?
① Vote on your own. → ② Briefly explain your reason in the chat. → ③ Read everyone's reasons and vote again.
You tested the lecture chatbot before release. You asked each of 20 prepared questions once, and every answer was correct. What should you do next?
A. Release it as is.
B. Ask the same questions several times, add unanswerable questions, and measure again.
C. Set temperature to its maximum for richer answers, then release.
D. Switch to the largest model, then release.
If you are reading the materials on your own, choose an answer before moving to the next slide. Try explaining your reason briefly.

content.title: Quiz 1: ready to release? — answer
content.content:
Quiz 1/4
Quiz 1: ready to release? — answer
Answer: B.
You tested the lecture chatbot before release. You asked each of 20 prepared questions once, and every answer was correct. What should you do next?
A. Release it as is.
B. Ask the same questions several times, add unanswerable questions, and measure again.
C. Set temperature to its maximum for richer answers, then release.
D. Switch to the largest model, then release.
Answers vary probabilistically, so a single correct answer may be luck. The model can also answer plausibly when it does not know. Measure multiple runs and include unanswerable questions.
The core of Part 1: both variation and errors result from probabilistic selection. Measure and manage them rather than assuming they can be eliminated.

content.title: Working with variation and errors
content.content:
1/4: LLMs select the next words probabilistically
Working with variation and errors
The principle of probabilistic selection determines what to check before release.
Practical guide 1/4
What to do | Why, from Part 1's principle
1. Ask the same question multiple times, for example five times each. | Answers vary probabilistically.
2. Choose and fix temperature for the purpose: lower for facts, higher for ideas. | The selection method changes the character of answers.
3. Include unanswerable questions and measure whether the model can say “I don't know”. | It gives plausible answers even without knowledge.
4. Require supporting sources and check that they really exist. | The model does not verify correctness itself.
5. Provide only relevant portions rather than entire documents. | It overlooks the middle of long contexts.
6. If the API exposes logprobs, flag low-probability answers for review. | This is a rough guide: probability and correctness may diverge.
Example lecture chatbot settings:
• Temperature: fixed at 0.2.
• Evaluation: 50 questions × 5 runs, including 10 questions whose answers are absent from the materials.
• Instruction: “If something is not in the materials, answer ‘I don't know’. Include the supporting slide number.”
• Materials: pass only three slides relevant to the question, using RAG.
Motto: do not trust one correct answer. Measure multiple runs, including unanswerable questions, before release.

content.section: Provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more

content.title: Provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more
content.content:
Lecture 2 — Part 2/4, approximately 15 minutes
Provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more.
When a chatbot does not answer as expected, where should we intervene in the model?

content.title: Choose the intervention according to the problem
content.content:
2/4: provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more
Choose the intervention according to the problem.
Model capabilities are built in three stages. Identifying which stage underlies the problem determines the intervention.
The core of these 15 minutes:
Provide information/select a model.
Pre-training determines the foundation of knowledge.
Problems: “It does not know the documents or new information; it is weak on specialist terms.”
Intervention: first provide documents using RAG. If the underlying foundation is insufficient, choose another model; see Part 3.
Adapt it.
Post-training determines how it answers.
Problems: “The format or tone is unsuitable; it does not include supporting evidence.”
Intervention: first use instructions, or prompts. If that does not fix it, use examples for FT; see Part 4.
Let it think more.
Inference-time compute brings out accuracy on difficult problems.
Problems: “It makes mistakes in calculations or complex explanations.”
Intervention: increase the thinking setting. This also increases cost and time.
Terminology: post-training is training after pre-training. Fine-Tuning, or FT, means doing post-training ourselves on a small scale.
Inference means using a trained model to answer. It differs from reasoning, meaning the act of thinking in a reasoning model.

content.title: Pre-training determines the knowledge foundation — so choose the model
content.content:
2/4: provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more
Pre-training determines the knowledge foundation — so choose the model.
Larger scale improves prediction: scaling laws. We cannot rebuild models at this scale ourselves.
Sources: J. Kaplan et al. (2020), Fig. 1; J. Hoffmann et al. (2022). Token counts are published figures with different counting conventions: Kimi K2 technical report (2025) and DeepSeek published figures.
Scaling laws, Kaplan et al. (2020): vertical axis = test loss, or next-token prediction error; horizontal axes = dataset size, parameter count and compute, on logarithmic scales.
If the other resources are sufficient, increasing any one regularly reduces error. Hoffmann et al. (2022) addresses optimal allocation. This is the basis of the race to scale.
The knowledge foundation is determined here. What we can do is choose the model; see Part 3.
Pre-training tokens, in trillions:
GPT-3 (2020): 0.3 trillion.
Kimi K2: 15.5 trillion.
DeepSeek-V4-Pro: 33 trillion.
About 110 times as many. Assuming 100,000 tokens per book, this is at least 25 times the entire National Diet Library collection, estimated at about 1.3 trillion tokens.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
Three chart horizontal axes: Dataset Size (tokens); Parameters (non-embedding); Compute (PF-days, non-embedding).
Vertical axis: Test Loss.

content.title: Knowledge has a cutoff: the model only knows up to its training data
content.content:
2/4: provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more
Knowledge has a cutoff: the model only knows up to the time of its training data.
It does not know events after pre-training ends. Including the period from release to use, the gap can be months to years.
A model's life, schematically: collect training data → cutoff (knowledge cutoff) → model release, months later → use it now, possibly more than a year later.
It does not know events during the period after the cutoff.
Training data contents: websites, books, papers, code and more. English is common; Japanese and specialist fields are relatively less represented.
For a chatbot:
• It does not know this year's syllabus or deadlines → provide the materials using RAG; Lecture 5.
• It is asked about new methods → choose a newer model or let it search.
• It is weak in Japanese or a specialist field → choose a model for Japanese or that domain.
• ChatGPT and similar services can answer about current topics because search results are placed in the input. The model's knowledge has not increased.

content.title: Post-training determines how the model answers — so we can adapt it
content.content:
2/4: provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more
Post-training determines how the model answers — so we can adapt it.
Teach a pre-trained model how to answer using examples and evaluation. Doing a small-scale version ourselves is Fine-Tuning.
Source: based on Iwasawa's 2026 Japan Logistics Society lecture materials, replacing the examples with the lecture chatbot.
Learning from examples — SFT:
Show question/ideal-answer pairs and have the model imitate how to answer.
Example: thousands of examples of “question → polite answer with supporting evidence”.
Learning from human preferences — RLHF:
People choose the better of two answers; the model learns this preference.
Example: prefer the clearer explanation.
Learning from automatic grading — RLVR:
Increase correct answers on tasks whose correctness can be judged by a machine.
Example: grade using answers to calculation problems or code test results.
For a chatbot, examples teach the pattern of answering politely with supporting evidence; human preferences improve clarity. Doing this ourselves at a small scale is Fine-Tuning; see Part 4.

content.title: Before and after post-training: the same question gets different behavior
content.content:
2/4: provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more
Before and after post-training: the same question gets different behavior.
A model with only pre-training writes a continuation of text. Post-training makes it answer questions.
Source: figure from L. Ouyang et al., “Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT)”, NeurIPS 2022, Fig. 2. The example on the left is illustrative.
Consider what a pre-trained-only model returns. Illustrative input: “What is RAG?”
Pre-trained-only model:
“What is RAG? How does RAG differ from LLMs? How do you implement RAG? …”
It writes the continuation of an FAQ list.
After post-training:
“RAG is a method that retrieves documents relevant to the question and builds an answer based on them.”
InstructGPT's three stages: examples → human ranking → reinforcement learning.
In human preference evaluations, 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT was preferred over 175-billion-parameter GPT-3.
This is a difference in how it answers, not an increase in knowledge — adaptation has value.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
InstructGPT figure:
Step 1 Collect demonstration data, and train a supervised policy.
Step 2 Collect comparison data, and train a reward model.
Step 3 Optimize a policy against the reward model using reinforcement learning.

content.title: Inference-time compute: thinking more improves difficult answers
content.content:
2/4: provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more
Inference-time compute: letting a model think when it is used makes it better at difficult problems.
Have it write intermediate reasoning, or CoT (Chain of Thought), or generate multiple candidates and select one. We can buy more capability without changing the model.
Sources: Wei et al., “Chain-of-Thought Prompting”, NeurIPS 2022, Fig. 1; OpenAI, “Learning to reason with LLMs”, 2024. o1 is OpenAI's reasoning model.
Writing intermediate reasoning (CoT): left, answer only → wrong; right, intermediate steps → correct.
Generating candidates and selecting: accuracy of the same o1 on the AIME mathematics competition.
Single answer: 74%. Select from 1,000 candidates: 93%.
The 93% result is a research setting in which a grader selects from 1,000 candidates. Compute is about 1,000 times higher.
APIs can let us choose how much the model thinks. budget_tokens is an upper limit on thinking; syntax varies by API and over time.
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-...",
    max_tokens=16000,
    thinking={"type": "enabled",
              "budget_tokens": 8000},
    messages=[...])
• Use more thinking selectively, for difficult questions.
• The tradeoff is greater cost in output tokens and longer waiting time.
• The small open model used in the exercise does not have this setting.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
Standard Prompting / Chain-of-Thought Prompting
Q: Roger has 5 tennis balls. He buys 2 more cans of tennis balls. Each can has 3 tennis balls. How many tennis balls does he have now?
Standard A: The answer is 11.
CoT A: Roger started with 5 balls. 2 cans of 3 tennis balls each is 6 tennis balls. 5 + 6 = 11. The answer is 11.
Q: The cafeteria had 23 apples. If they used 20 to make lunch and bought 6 more, how many apples do they have?
Standard A: The answer is 27. [Marked incorrect in the figure.]
CoT A: The cafeteria had 23 apples originally. They used 20 to make lunch. So they had 23 - 20 = 3. They bought 6 more apples, so they have 3 + 6 = 9. The answer is 9.

Quiz 2: where should you intervene?
① Vote on your own. → ② Briefly explain your reason in the chat. → ③ Read everyone's reasons and vote again.
When asked about a new method announced this year, the chatbot answers with old information. What should you try first?
A. Raise temperature to produce more diverse answers.
B. Increase thinking, or inference-time compute.
C. Retrieve and provide new materials. If necessary, choose a newer model.
D. Fine-tune the model to improve its tone.
If you are reading the materials on your own, choose an answer before moving to the next slide. Try explaining your reason briefly.

content.title: Quiz 2: where should you intervene? — answer
content.content:
Quiz 2/4
Quiz 2: where should you intervene? — answer
Answer: C.
When asked about a new method announced this year, the chatbot answers with old information. What should you try first?
A. Raise temperature to produce more diverse answers.
B. Increase thinking, or inference-time compute.
C. Retrieve and provide new materials. If necessary, choose a newer model.
D. Fine-tune the model to improve its tone.
The cause is the knowledge cutoff. Thinking more cannot produce what it does not know. Provide materials using RAG, or choose a newer model. Letting it search is the same intervention; see Lecture 3.
The core of Part 2: the problem determines where to intervene. For knowledge, provide information or select a model; for answer behavior, adapt it, starting with prompts; for difficult problems, let it think more.

content.title: Find the intervention from the symptom
content.content:
2/4: provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more
Find the intervention from the symptom.
Use the symptom to identify the stage causing the problem. This determines both the intervention and the lecture that covers it in detail.
Practical guide 2/4
Symptom → intervention | Cause
1. Does not know new information or document contents → provide documents through RAG, let it search, or choose a newer model. | Pre-training: knowledge cutoff.
2. Unnatural specialist terminology or Japanese → select a Japanese/domain-specific model. | Pre-training: data bias.
3. Does not follow the format, tone or procedure → first prompts; if they fail, FT. | Post-training: how it answers.
4. Mistakes on difficult problems → increase thinking or use a reasoning model. | Inference-time compute.
5. Slow or expensive → smaller model, FT, or less thinking. | Overall cost.
Covered in detail:
• RAG: Lecture 5.
• Searching with agents: Lecture 3.
• Prompts: Lecture 9.
• Fine-Tuning: today's Part 4.
• Model selection: today's Part 3.
• Evaluation sets: Lecture 4.
In every case, use an evaluation set to check whether the problem was fixed; Lecture 4.

content.title: The second half: choosing and adapting foundation models
content.content:
2/4: provide information/select a model, adapt it, or let it think more
The second half: examine “choosing” and “adapting” foundation models in more detail.
Every intervention starts by choosing a model. If problems with how it answers remain, adapt it at the end. This adaptation is today's exercise.
Interventions covered in more detail elsewhere:
Measure, using evaluation sets — Lecture 4.
Provide information, using RAG — Lecture 5.
Let it use tools, through agents — Lecture 3.
Improve instructions, or prompts — Lecture 9.
Let it think more, using inference-time compute — covered in Part 2.
Choose — Part 3: which foundation models exist and which to use. The deciding factors are your own evaluation and “cost < benefit”.
Adapt — Part 4, then the exercise: when the selected model's answer behavior is unsuitable, when should you use FT and how?

content.section: A map of foundation models and how to choose

content.title: A map of foundation models and how to choose
content.content:
Lecture 2 — Part 3/4, approximately 15 minutes
A map of foundation models and how to choose
What foundation models exist beyond LLMs, and how should we choose and use them?

content.title: Foundation models are not only for language: choose using a map
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Foundation models are not only for language: choose using a map.
The core of these 15 minutes: language, images, audio, time series and more each have established foundation models for their input/output types. Decide using your own evaluation set.
Map: organize models according to what they take as input and produce as output.
Many are publicly available models. Find them on Hugging Face and try them with a few lines of code.
Choose the cheapest, fastest model that is sufficient for the task, rather than the strongest model.

content.title: Foundation model map: inputs and outputs
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Foundation model map: inputs and outputs
A representation, or vector, is data expressed as a sequence of numbers. Similar meanings have nearby values, which is useful for search and classification.
Language, or LLM: text → text. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Qwen, Llama.
Image/text alignment: image and text → a shared representation. CLIP, SigLIP.
Image feature extraction: image → representation. DINOv3.
Segmentation: image + instruction → region. SAM, SAM 2, SAM 3.
VLM: image + text → text. Qwen-VL, Gemma, InternVL.
Image/video generation: text → image/video. Stable Diffusion, FLUX.
Audio: speech ↔ text. Whisper.
Embeddings for search: text → vector. BGE-M3, E5, which serve as the retriever in RAG.
Time series: past → future forecast. Chronos, TimesFM.
Robotics, or VLA (vision, language, action): image + instruction → action. π0, OpenVLA.

content.title: Open LLMs: commonly used model families
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Open LLMs: commonly used model families
These are open-weight models whose weights are public. Training data and code are not necessarily public. Always check the license to determine whether commercial use is permitted.
Sources: official sites and Hugging Face, checked in October 2026. Family names are used because versions change frequently.
Qwen — Alibaba: many size choices; strong multilingual performance; a common FT base.
Llama — Meta: sparked the open LLM movement; extensive surrounding tools and information.
Gemma — Google: small to medium models, easier to run on local PCs and smartphones.
gpt-oss — OpenAI: released in 2025; an open model strong in reasoning.
DeepSeek — DeepSeek: large-scale MoE, an architecture that computes only necessary parts; see the appendix. Attracted attention with the reasoning model R1.
Kimi and GLM — Moonshot AI and Z.ai: includes trillion-parameter-class MoEs; prominent in agent applications.
Japanese models — LLM-jp, Swallow and others: released by Japanese research institutions with strengthened Japanese capabilities.

content.title: Image foundation models: CLIP, DINO and SAM
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Image foundation models: CLIP, DINO and SAM
Linking images and words, extracting features focused on objects, and segmenting objects: these are building blocks of many image AI systems.
Sources: figures from Radford et al., “CLIP”, 2021; Caron et al., “DINO”, 2021; Kirillov et al., “SAM”, 2023, via their respective GitHub repositories. DINOv3: August 2025; SAM 3: November 2025.
CLIP / SigLIP — images and words in the same space:
• Classify and search without additional training, or zero-shot, using similarity to text such as “a photo of a dog”.
• Also used as the eyes of VLMs.
DINO, most recently DINOv3 — learn object-focused features without labels:
• Focuses on object shapes even without being explicitly taught to do so.
• A foundation for detection, segmentation and more. The backbone is the feature-extracting component.
SAM, or Segment Anything — segment the specified object:
• Specify a point or box → output a region. SAM 2 supports video.
• SAM 3 also accepts text such as “yellow bus”.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
CLIP diagram: Image Encoder; Text Encoder; (2) Create dataset classifier from label text; (3) Use for zero-shot prediction.

content.title: VLMs: LLMs that can read images
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
VLMs: LLMs that can read images
An image encoder, such as a CLIP-based encoder, converts images into tokens, which an LLM reads together with text.
Source: example adapted and summarized from H. Liu et al., “Visual Instruction Tuning (LLaVA)”, NeurIPS 2023. Image from the LLaVA repository.
Image → image encoder, CLIP-based → image tokens + question → LLM → text answer.
Consider: can AI identify what is unusual in this image? Example from the LLaVA paper.
Question: What is unusual about this image?
VLM: A man has set up an ironing board and is ironing at the back of a moving car. This task is normally done indoors and is dangerous on the road.
For a chatbot: a student can paste an image of a slide and ask what the figure means.
Common open VLMs include the Qwen-VL family, Gemma, InternVL and Molmo.

content.title: Audio and generation: Whisper and diffusion models
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Audio and generation: Whisper and diffusion models
Models that turn speech into text, and models that generate images/video from noise: both are established building blocks.
Sources: figures from A. Radford et al., “Whisper”, 2022, via GitHub; J. Ho et al., “Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models”, NeurIPS 2020, Fig. 2.
Whisper: speech → text.
Trained on about 680,000 hours of speech and transcripts. Supports multilingual transcription and translation.
Chatbot use: transcribe lecture recordings to create searchable materials for RAG.
Diffusion models: noise → image.
Gradually move from the noise on the left to the image on the right. Learn the reverse of adding noise to an image, then generate an image from noise.
Stable Diffusion and FLUX use this idea; video generation also uses the same approach.
Lecture uses include creating diagrams and illustrations for teaching materials.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
Whisper diagram: Multitask training data (680k hours); sequence-to-sequence learning; Multitask training format.

content.title: Time-series foundation models: predicting the future from past values
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Time-series foundation models: predicting the future from past values
Pre-training on large amounts of time-series data allows prediction on previously unseen data without additional training, or zero-shot.
Sources: A. F. Ansari et al., “Chronos”, TMLR 2024, Fig. 1; Google TimesFM and Salesforce Moirai official materials, checked October 2026.
Chronos, Ansari et al., Fig. 1: convert numbers to tokens and learn as an LLM does.
Left: divide past values into tokens. Middle: train to predict the next token. Right: convert predictions back into numbers, sampling multiple possible futures.
The same next-token prediction mechanism used in LLMs also works for time series.
Chronos — Amazon.
TimesFM — Google.
Moirai — Salesforce.
TimeGPT — Nixtla, via API.
Use cases include demand, traffic counts and sensor values. Always compare with conventional methods too.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
Chronos diagram: Time Series Tokenization; Training; Inference; Time Series Language Model.

content.title: Where to obtain and run models: three choices
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Where to obtain and run models: three choices
Call an API, run an open-weight model in the cloud, or run it locally.
Call an API:
• OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others.
• Access to the latest and highest-performing models.
• No setup; pay for what you use.
• Data is sent outside your environment.
• Subject to changes in prices and specifications.
Run an open model in the cloud:
• Hugging Face hosts a large number of models.
• Examples: Llama, Qwen, Gemma.
• Can be adapted to your needs through FT.
• Requires effort to prepare and operate GPUs.
• May not reach the performance of the strongest API models.
Run locally:
• Small language models, or SLMs, can run on your own PC.
• Data stays local.
• Works without network communication.
• Model size is limited.
• Speed depends on PC performance.
The preparatory homework and exercise use the middle option: an open model on Colab exposed through an API we build ourselves, distinct from vendors' APIs.

content.title: Choose with your own evaluation set, not benchmark rankings
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Choose with your own evaluation set, not benchmark rankings.
Public benchmark conditions differ across companies and do not reveal performance on your use case.
What public benchmarks tell you:
• Rough comparisons of model capability.
• General abilities in mathematics, code, specialist knowledge and other areas.
• However, evaluation conditions such as tools and compute differ across companies, so rankings cannot simply be compared directly.
• The model may have seen the test questions during training — effectively a form of cheating.
What your own evaluation set tells you:
• Accuracy on lecture questions, using real questions.
• Whether the model says “I don't know” to unanswerable questions.
• Cost and waiting time per question.
We cover how to build evaluation sets in Lecture 4.

content.title: Cost below benefit is decisive: lower costs expand applications
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
The deciding factor is “cost < benefit”. Lower costs expand the range of applications.
Only applications whose benefit per item exceeds the cost are used in practice. Lowering the cost expands that range.
Sources: Jevons, The Coal Question, 1865; Stanford HAI AI Index 2025, at performance equivalent to 64.8% on MMLU, November 2022 → October 2024; Epoch AI.
Schematic: arrange applications from highest to lowest benefit per item:
Explaining difficult problems → answering questions → summarizing documents → casual conversation.
Previous cost; current cost.
Legend: applications already viable; applications made viable by lower costs.
Jevons paradox: when the unit price falls, total usage can increase instead. Originally discussed for coal in 1865.
For LLMs too:
• The price of GPT-3.5-equivalent performance fell to about 1/280 in roughly two years, 2022 → 2024. Usage also rose rapidly.
• However, reasoning models increase tokens per request by orders of magnitude.
Two approaches:
• Reduce cost through model selection, FT in Part 4, and adjusting the amount of thinking.
• Apply the model where the benefit is large.

content.title: Routine decisions: a small classifier plus a program is fast and cheap
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Routine decisions: a small classifier plus a program is fast and cheap.
Examples: embeddings + a classifier; FT of a small model; a model specialized in classification, such as TypeSafe AI's Jev, announced in September 2026.
Sources: TypeSafe AI's Jev announcement, September 15, 2026; nasuvitz's Qiita article, 2026. Probabilities are illustrative.
Illustrative chatbot example:
Student: “I don't know where to submit my report.”
Specialized model output, values with probabilities:
Type: administrative procedure 0.93; lecture content 0.05; other 0.02.
Urgency: 0.71.
Administrative procedure → return standard guidance.
Lecture content → answer with RAG + LLM.
Other → route to a staff member.
Who decides the next operation: the program or AI?
Specialized model + program | LLM-centered agent
Delegated to AI: classification, judgment and grading | interpretation of the situation and selection of the next action.
Next operation: code conditionals decide | the LLM chooses based on conversation and tool results.
Suitable situations: recurring fixed decisions; fast, cheap and easy to explain | work requiring different responses according to the situation, covered in Lecture 3.
Jev is named after Jevons. Its design aims to make more applications viable through lower cost and greater speed.

content.title: Quiz 3: routing 10,000 inquiries per day
content.content:
Quiz 3/4
Quiz 3: routing 10,000 inquiries per day
① Vote on your own. → ② Briefly explain your reason in the chat. → ③ Read everyone's reasons and vote again.

content.title: Steps for choosing a model
content.content:
3/4: a map of foundation models and how to choose
Steps for choosing a model
Use the map to choose the type, write down your constraints, and compare candidates with your own evaluation.
Practical guide 3/4
Step | Why, from Part 3's principle
1. Define inputs and outputs, then choose the model type from the map. | Each type has established models.
2. Write constraints: permission to send data externally, budget, speed and language. | This determines which of the three access options is suitable.
3. Choose about three candidates: API, open or specialized models. | You need a comparison to know.
4. Measure accuracy, cost and latency using your own evaluation set. | Benchmark rankings are not a reliable basis.
5. Select the cheapest model satisfying “cost < benefit”. | Lower cost expands possible uses.
6. Reconsider every six months. | Models and prices change quickly.
Example lecture chatbot constraints:
• Data: check university rules on whether lecture materials may be sent to external APIs.
• Budget: at most ¥1 per question. At the appendix's hypothetical prices, a large model costs about ¥2 and a small model about ¥0.2.
• Speed: begin answering within three seconds.
• Language: Japanese lecture materials.
Decide using accuracy, cost and speed on your use case, rather than ranking.

content.section: When and how to adapt the selected model

content.title: When and how should you adapt the selected model?
content.content:
Lecture 2 — Part 4/4, approximately 15 minutes
When and how should you adapt the selected model?
Even the selected model answers in an unsuitable way. Should you use Fine-Tuning or another method?

content.title: Small-scale FT changes behavior well but is weaker at adding knowledge
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
Small-scale FT changes behavior well but is weaker at adding knowledge.
The core of these 15 minutes: for behavior that prompts cannot fix, try Fine-Tuning. For knowledge, first try retrieval through RAG.
Behavior: output format, tone and following procedures. A small number of examples can change it.
Knowledge: new facts and current materials. Memorizing them through FT is inefficient, and some studies report increased errors.
Cost: if short prompts and a small model can produce the same behavior, the system becomes faster and cheaper.

content.title: Evidence and debate: RAG often works better for adding knowledge
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
Evidence and debate: RAG often works better for adding knowledge.
This does not mean FT can add no knowledge at all. Treat it as a general rule while understanding the exceptions.
Sources: Ovadia et al., EMNLP 2024; Gekhman et al., EMNLP 2024; Biderman et al., TMLR 2024; Zhou et al., LIMA, NeurIPS 2023.
Research findings underlying the general rule:
Ovadia et al. (2024): on knowledge tasks, RAG consistently outperformed FT directly on documents.
Gekhman et al. (2024): examples containing new knowledge are learned slowly; learning more of them tends to increase errors, or hallucinations.
Biderman et al. (2024): LoRA learns less and forgets less than full FT. It suits small adjustments.
Exceptions and differing findings:
• Continued pre-training, or CPT, on large amounts of text can add language and domain knowledge, as in Japanese Swallow models.
• Training on varied paraphrases of the same fact can make knowledge easier to learn through FT.
• About 1,000 high-quality examples can substantially change behavior, as in LIMA.
• Transferring a large model's behavior to a small one, or distillation, is also used to reduce cost and latency.

content.title: Continued pre-training: adding knowledge and language
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
Continued pre-training (CPT): additional training to add knowledge and language.
Continue next-token prediction on domain text itself, rather than question-and-answer examples.
Sources: Swallow, Institute of Science Tokyo and AIST; AIRoA (2026), and others; S. Gururangan et al., “Don't Stop Pretraining”, ACL 2020.
A common training sequence:
Pre-trained model → continued pre-training on domain text → SFT for instruction following → RL and evaluation to shape behavior.
Suitable when:
• You want broad domain vocabulary and knowledge, such as medicine, law or Japanese.
• You have much text but no question/answer examples.
Requirements:
• Billions to hundreds of billions of tokens of text.
• Many GPUs and substantial training/evaluation effort.
Cautions:
• Original capabilities can be forgotten; mix in general text.
• SFT is needed afterward for instruction following.
• Unsuitable for frequently changing information.
Examples: Swallow adds Japanese through continued pre-training of Llama and other models; AIRoA addresses robotics. It also supports domain adaptation in medicine, law and other fields.

content.title: FT is also used to reduce cost
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
FT is also used to reduce cost.
Teaching the model instructions and examples can shorten prompts and let a smaller model produce the same behavior.
Source: illustrative estimate, using the appendix's hypothetical prices per million tokens: large model, input $3 and output $15; small model, input $0.25 and output $1.25.
Consider: how much cheaper does FT make 200 questions per lecture?
Before FT: large model + long prompt.
Input 3,100 tokens: instructions 1,000 + examples 2,000 + question 100. Output 500 tokens.
About $3.4.
After FT: fine-tuned small model + short prompt.
Input 200 tokens: instructions 100 + question 100. Output 500 tokens.
About $0.14.
Whether to use FT depends on “cost < benefit”:
Savings per question × number of questions > FT cost, including creating examples, training and evaluation.
• This course alone, 13 lectures: saves about $42. Creating examples takes more effort than the saving warrants.
• University-wide, 100 times the scale: about $4,200. FT begins to be worthwhile.
However, repeated long instructions may also become cheaper through API prompt caching, which reuses identical portions at a discount. Some services charge more per token for fine-tuned models than for the original model. Compare actual prices.

content.title: Decision sequence: measure, separate, prompt, then Fine-Tuning
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
Decision sequence: measure → separate the problem → prompts → Fine-Tuning.
This makes Lecture 1's broad classification of models and methods concrete. Start with approaches that are cheap and quick to try, checking each with evaluation.
1. First create an evaluation set, so you can measure whether the problem is fixed. Lecture 4.
2. Do you want to change knowledge or behavior? For knowledge, retrieve and provide information with RAG. Lecture 5.
3. Can prompts, including instructions and examples, fix it? If so, that is sufficient. Lecture 9.
4. Does an unwanted behavior still remain? Consider Fine-Tuning.

content.title: PEFT: train only part of a model
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
PEFT: train only part of a model, not the whole model.
FT that updates every parameter is expensive. Methods that train only a small number of parameters, or PEFT, have become mainstream.
Sources: original papers by Houlsby et al. (2019), Li and Liang (2021), Lester et al. (2021), and Hu et al. (2022). Available through the Hugging Face PEFT library.
What is trained, Dettmers et al., Fig. 1:
Full Fine-Tuning: update all parameters; large memory and storage requirements.
LoRA: freeze the base model and update only a small added component.
QLoRA: also compress the base model to 4 bits to save memory.
Main PEFT methods:
Adapters: insert small layers between existing layers and train only those. Houlsby et al., 2019.
Prefix/prompt tuning: prepend trainable virtual tokens to the input. Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021.
LoRA: represent and learn weight changes as the product of two small, thin matrices, a low-rank representation. Hu et al., 2022. Currently the most widely used approach.
QLoRA: LoRA plus compression of original weights to 4 bits for even lower memory use. Dettmers et al., 2023; next slide.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
Comparison diagram: Full Finetuning (No Adapters) / LoRA / QLoRA.
Optimizer; Adapters; 16-bit Transformer; 4-bit Transformer.

content.title: LoRA and QLoRA: adapting a large model on one GPU
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
LoRA and QLoRA: adapting a large model on one GPU
Freeze the original weights and train only a small change, or delta, with LoRA. QLoRA also compresses the original weights to 4 bits.
Sources: E. J. Hu et al., “LoRA”, ICLR 2022; T. Dettmers et al., “QLoRA”, NeurIPS 2023. The exercise uses transformers, peft, bitsandbytes and TRL.
LoRA, Hu et al., Fig. 1: train only A and B.
Blue — original weights W: frozen, not trained. QLoRA stores them at 4 bits, a coarser numerical representation, reducing memory to about one quarter. About 4 GB for 7B.
Orange — small matrices A and B: only these are trained. The product of two thin matrices represents the change, with low rank.
Analogy: leave the main model unchanged and add thin sticky notes. The trainable portion can be less than 1% of the total.
The QLoRA paper fine-tuned a 65-billion-parameter model on one 48 GB GPU.
• Even a Colab GPU, for example 16 GB, can adapt a model with billions of parameters. This is today's exercise.
• Data preparation, evaluation and operation still require separate effort.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
LoRA diagram: Pretrained Weights W ∈ R^(d×d); x; h; A ~ N(0, σ²); B = 0; d; r.

content.title: For a chatbot: what to fine-tune and what not to
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
For a chatbot: what to fine-tune and what not to
This is the topic of today's exercise. In practice, first try prompts and the API's format controls.
Use FT to change output format. We want the model always to return this JSON format:
{
  "answer": "RAG retrieves documents and…",
  "slide": 13,
  "confidence": "high"
}
FT does not fix the knowledge problem: questions such as “Which GPU is used in the Lecture 2 exercise?” depend on facts found only in the materials. FT is unlikely to make them answerable.
→ Retrieve and provide the materials with RAG; Lecture 5.
The examples in this exercise contain no facts, so knowledge is naturally not expected to increase. Measure this to verify it.
We use JSON in the exercise because its effect is easy to count. In practice, first use API structured output when you only need to enforce a format. FT helps with behavior a format cannot enforce, such as tone or how evidence is presented.

content.title: Building examples: pair questions with ideal answers
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
Building examples: pair questions with ideal answers.
For correcting format, start with a few hundred examples. Quality matters more than quantity. Always set evaluation data aside separately.
Sources: C. Zhou et al., “LIMA”, NeurIPS 2023; Z. Gekhman et al., EMNLP 2024. Counts are rough guides.
train.jsonl: one line per example. This one-record example is displayed with indentation for readability:
{"messages": [
  {"role": "system", "content": "Answer lecture questions. Reply in JSON"},
  {"role": "user", "content": "What is LoRA?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "{\"answer\": \"…\", \"slide\": 52, \"confidence\": \"high\"}"}
]}
One example = instruction + question + ideal answer. Prepare hundreds to thousands of these.
Keep the format, tone and method of citing evidence consistent, rather than focusing on answer content.
Number: start with hundreds for correcting format. LIMA reports substantial behavior changes with 1,000 high-quality examples.
Diversity: cover a wide range of phrasings close to real questions. Do not include incorrect examples.
Do not add knowledge: teaching new facts through examples tends to increase errors, according to Gekhman et al.
Keep separate: separate training from evaluation data. Never train on evaluation questions.

content.title: FT pitfalls: did anything else break?
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
FT pitfalls: did anything other than the target behavior break?
Measure both the metric you want to improve and the metrics you do not want to harm, before and after FT.
Forgetting original capabilities: answers to ordinary questions or the naturalness of Japanese worsen. Example: explanations suddenly become worse.
Overfitting to examples: every request gets JSON and the same phrases recur. Example: even “Hello” gets JSON.
Cheating on evaluation: evaluation questions enter the training examples and only the score improves. Example: real production questions remain unfixed.
Rework: each new base model requires reviewing examples and retraining. Example: more work every six months.
In the exercise too, compare both format compliance, which you want to improve, and answers to ordinary questions, which you do not want to harm, before and after FT.

content.title: Quiz 4: what is Fine-Tuning best suited for?
content.content:
Quiz 4/4
Quiz 4: what is Fine-Tuning best suited for?
① Vote on your own. → ② Briefly explain your reason in the chat. → ③ Read everyone's reasons and vote again.
There are four things you want to improve in the lecture chatbot. Which is Fine-Tuning best suited for?
A. Correctly answering assignment deadlines that change every year.
B. Always returning answers in a fixed JSON format.
C. Learning new content discussed in today's lecture.
D. Improving accuracy on difficult calculation problems.
If you are reading the materials on your own, choose an answer before moving to the next slide. Try explaining your reason briefly.

content.title: Quiz 4: what is Fine-Tuning best suited for? — answer
content.content:
Quiz 4/4
Quiz 4: what is Fine-Tuning best suited for? — answer
Answer: B.
There are four things you want to improve in the lecture chatbot. Which is Fine-Tuning best suited for?
A. Correctly answering assignment deadlines that change every year.
B. Always returning answers in a fixed JSON format.
C. Learning new content discussed in today's lecture.
D. Improving accuracy on difficult calculation problems.
Format is behavior, so examples can change it. In practice, first try prompts or structured output. A and C concern knowledge, so use RAG; D calls for inference-time compute or model selection.
The core of Part 4: use FT for behavior; for knowledge, try RAG first. FT is also used to reduce cost.

content.title: Checklist before Fine-Tuning
content.content:
4/4: when and how to adapt the selected model
Checklist before Fine-Tuning
Proceed to FT once all six items have a checkmark.
Practical guide 4/4
Check | Why, from Part 4's principle
1. You have an evaluation set separate from training data. | You cannot decide without measuring whether the problem is fixed.
2. You want to change behavior — format, tone or procedure — rather than knowledge. | FT adds knowledge poorly and can increase errors.
3. Prompts, format controls and RAG did not fix it. | Start with approaches that are cheap and quick to try.
4. You can prepare at least hundreds of examples with consistent quality. | Example quality determines behavior.
5. Savings × volume, or benefit, exceeds FT cost, including retraining. | Cost < benefit.
6. You plan to measure capabilities you do not want to harm, before and after. | Forgetting and overfitting occur.
If all are checked, start small:
• Start with LoRA/QLoRA and a smaller model.
• Start with hundreds of examples; add more if needed.
• Run the same evaluation before and after, recording what improved and what did not.
• Today's exercise is a small-scale version of this workflow.
If even one item fails, first return to evaluation-set construction, prompts or RAG.

content.title: Today's exercise: correct output format with QLoRA and measure the effect
content.content:
Exercise
Today's exercise: correct output format with QLoRA and measure the effect.
Continue from the preparatory homework: exposing a model through an API using Colab + FastAPI + ngrok, and observing variation caused by temperature.
Prepare: resolve difficulties from the preparatory homework.
Measure before: measure format compliance, repeating runs at the same temperature.
Train with QLoRA: fine-tune using examples that follow the required format.
Measure after: replace the model with the fine-tuned version and measure using the same questions.
Control — knowledge questions: these should not change. If they do, question the evaluation.
Format compliance rate = the proportion of answers that can be parsed as JSON and contain all required fields: answer, slide and confidence.
You can say the issue was fixed only after running the same evaluation before and after.

content.title: Exercise steps and deliverables — tentative
content.content:
Exercise
Exercise steps and deliverables — tentative
Times are approximate. It is important to use the same questions, temperature and number of runs before and after.
1. Preparation, 10 minutes: fix problems from the preparatory homework and check that the API works.
2. Measure before FT, 10 minutes: use 30 evaluation questions × 3 runs to measure format compliance. Also save answers to 10 ordinary questions.
3. Train with QLoRA, 20 minutes: train on 200 examples, taking roughly ten to twenty minutes on a Colab GPU.
4. Measure after FT, 10 minutes: replace the model and use the same questions, temperature and number of runs as in step 2.
5. Control — knowledge questions, 5 minutes: the examples include no facts, so the results should not change. If they do, suspect an evaluation or training error.
Deliverables:
• A before/after comparison table: format compliance and answers to ordinary questions.
• Two examples of questions that were not fixed.
• A three-line discussion of what improved, what did not, and why.
Use 30 evaluation questions that do not overlap with training data. Small differences may be within the noise, so report variation across the three runs too.

content.title: Next: AI agents — today's properties are design assumptions
content.content:
Next lecture
Next: AI agents. Today's properties become design assumptions.
An agent adds tools, a loop and memory to today's model so it can act: the outer layer in the diagram on slide 5.
What we learned | How it matters for agents
Probabilistic selection and varied answers | The same request may lead to different steps each time. Do not trust one success; measure multiple runs.
Plausible errors | It may call nonexistent tools or misread results. We need mechanisms to check results and conditions for stopping.
Uneven use of long contexts | In long tasks, earlier instructions and results can be missed. Memory needs organization.
Format compliance, as in today's exercise | Tool calls use fixed formats such as JSON. The ability to follow a format is foundational.
Cost < benefit | More loops mean more tokens. Decide what to leave to AI and what the program should determine.

content.title: Deep learning basics: stack layers and reduce prediction error
content.content:
Appendix
Deep learning basics: stack layers and reduce the gap between predictions and correct answers.
Both multiple regression and deep learning adjust internal coefficients, or weights/parameters, to reduce this gap.
Source: Iwasawa's 2026 Japan Logistics Society lecture materials. Figures: neural network schematic; layer-wise features from Goodfellow et al., Deep Learning, 2016; backpropagation schematic.
A computational structure of stacked layers: repeatedly combine additions and nonlinear transformations to represent complex relationships.
Features are built layer by layer: for images, edges → corners and parts → objects, becoming progressively more abstract.
Training = adjusting coefficients: use the gap between prediction and correct answer to calculate how to change each layer's coefficients, working backward through the network. This is backpropagation.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
Neural network diagram: input layer → hidden layer 1 → hidden layer 2 → output layer.

content.title: Self-attention: calculating where each token focuses in the text
content.content:
Appendix
Self-attention: calculating where each token focuses in the text.
This is the central mechanism of the Transformer. It can identify what “it” refers to from the whole context.
Sources: diagram based on a Google Research Blog visualization, 2017; Vaswani et al., NeurIPS 2017. Attention visualization is one possible interpretation.
How to read the diagram:
• The darkness of a line from “it” above to each word below indicates attention strength.
• The strongest attention goes to “animal”, showing the interpretation that “it” refers to the animal.
Connection to the main lecture:
• Multiple layers of these attention calculations produce next-token probabilities.
• How attention is assigned also depends on coefficients adjusted during training.

[Additional transcription of text in figures/images]
Attention diagram sentence: The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired.
Highlighted token: it.

content.title: MoE: a large model need not compute every part on every request
content.content:
Appendix
MoE: a large model need not compute every part on every request.
It uses only some experts for each input to make computation more efficient, as in DeepSeek-V4-Pro.
Source: based on Iwasawa's 2026 Japan Logistics Society lecture materials.
Input → selection mechanism, or router → Expert 1 / Expert 2 / Expert 3 / Expert 4 / Expert 5 / Expert 6.
Only some experts are used. Even with a large total parameter count, computation per pass can be limited.

content.title: How APIs work: send text and receive a continuation
content.content:
Appendix
How APIs work: send text and receive a continuation.
Charges depend on input and output token counts. Output, including inference-time compute, often has a higher unit price.
chatbot_api.py
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # API key comes from an environment variable
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-...",
    max_tokens=500,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}])
print(msg.content[0].text, msg.usage)
Returned information: answer text + token usage, or usage.
Token count multiplied by unit price gives the cost.
Request: model name, instructions, conversation history, maximum token count, temperature and other settings.
Response: generated text and counts of input/output tokens.
Caution: keep API keys secret. Request-count and token-count limits, or rate limits, apply.

LLM: it only writes the continuation or reply to a message
LLMs (large language models) are stateless (they keep no state).
Input
Run it and fix the failing test.
def total(n):
    return sum(range(1, n))
def test_total():
    assert total(4) == 10
LLM
Continues the text
Output (reply)
range(1, n) does not
include n.
Changing it to range(1, n + 1)
