content.section: Chapter 1: Hallucination and the limits of weights

content.title: Chapter 1: Hallucination and the limits of weights
content.content:
Chapter 1
Hallucination and the limits of weights
Hallucination / long-tail knowledge / parametric knowledge / fine-tuning

content.title: Rarer facts, lower accuracy
content.content:
Rarer facts, lower accuracy
• Fewer related pre-training documents → lower accuracy on that fact
• The trend holds as models grow
• Long-tail knowledge needs models orders of magnitude larger
Source: Kandpal et al. (2023) [9]. Figure from Kandpal et al. (2023) [9], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: BLOOM Model. Vertical axis: QA Accuracy. Horizontal axis: Number of Relevant Pre-training Documents. Legend: 176B / 7.1B / 3B / 1.7B / 1.1B / 560M.

content.title: Guessing when it does not know
content.content:
Guessing when it doesn't know
• If facts can't be told from errors, errors arise statistically
• Evals score “I don't know” as 0. Guessing scores higher
• So, even when unsure, it gives plausible wrong answers (hallucination)
Source: Kalai et al. (2025) [10]. Figure from Kalai et al. (2025) [10], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Valid examples +: Greetings. / How can I help? / There are 2 D’s in LADDER. / There is 1 N in PIANO. / Mia Holdner’s birthday is 4/1. / I don’t know Zdan’s birthday.
Error examples −: Greatings. / How kan eye help? / There are 3 L’s in SPELL. / There is 1 G in CAT. / Colin Merivale’s birthday is 8/29. / Jago Pere’s birthday is 8/21.
Right-hand figure: Spelling (good model) / Counting (poor model) / Birthdays (no pattern).

content.title: Adding to weights: slow, with side effects
content.content:
Adding to weights: slow, with side effects
• New-knowledge examples are learned far slower than known ones
• Memorizing more unknown examples lowers accuracy on other questions
• Knowledge in weights (parametric knowledge) comes from pre-training. Fine-tuning teaches how to use it
Source: Gekhman et al. (2024) [11]. Figure from Gekhman et al. (2024) [11], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: Train Accuracy / Dev Accuracy. Legend: Train Known / Train Unknown. Horizontal axis: Epochs. Overfitting starts.

content.title: Adding knowledge to weights is hard
content.content:
Adding knowledge to weights is hard

Difficulty | Details
Slow learning | New knowledge is learned more slowly than known knowledge
Adverse effects elsewhere | Memorizing more reduces accuracy on other questions
Requires a large amount of data | Facts with few relevant documents cannot be answered
Retraining for each update | Repeat training whenever knowledge changes

Relying on fine-tuning to add knowledge is hard
Source: Gekhman et al. (2024) [11], Kandpal et al. (2023) [9]

content.title: Chapter 2: Why RAG works: ICL
content.content:
Chapter 2
Why RAG works: ICL
In-Context Learning (ICL) / few-shot / RAG / non-parametric knowledge

content.title: ICL: learning from input, weights unchanged
content.content:
ICL: learning from input, weights unchanged
Give instructions + a few examples; predict the continuation to solve the task

Setting | What is supplied | Gradient update
Zero-shot | Task description only | None
One-shot | Description + 1 example | None
Few-shot | Description + a few to a few dozen examples | None
Fine-tuning | Train the weights on many examples | Yes

The GPT-3 paper named it In-Context Learning
Source: Brown et al. (2020) [12]. Table based on Figure 2.1

content.title: Solving tasks just by adding examples
content.content:
Solving tasks just by adding examples
• Task: remove extra symbols mixed into a word
• More examples raise accuracy; larger models show a steeper increase
Source: Brown et al. (2020) [12]. Figure from Brown et al. (2020) [12], Figure 1.2

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: Zero-shot / Natural Language Prompt / No Prompt. Vertical axis: Accuracy (%). Horizontal axis: Number of Examples in Context (K). Legend: 175B Params / 13B Params / 1.3B Params.

content.title: RAG: just add documents to the context
content.content:
RAG: just add documents to the context
• Just prepend retrieved documents to the input. Weights unchanged
• Inspired by ICL's success; named In-Context RALM
• An off-the-shelf retriever alone yields an improvement equivalent to increasing the parameter count by 2–3×
Source: Ram et al. (2023) [13]. Figure from Ram et al. (2023) [13], Figure 2

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Input: World Cup 2022 was the last with 32 teams, before the increase to
Document fetched by the Retriever: FIFA World Cup 2026 will expand to 48 teams.
Concatenate retrieved document and input → Language Model → 48 in the 2026 tournament.

content.title: RAG is noisy ICL
content.content:
RAG is noisy ICL
• Treat retrieved passages as noisy in-context examples
• Results include passages lacking the answer or wrong ones
• More retrieved examples: gains shrink, may turn negative
Source: Guo et al. (2025) [14]. Figure from Guo et al. (2025) [14], Figure 1. Theory in a linear-regression setting

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: NQ dataset / TriviaQA dataset. Vertical axis: Exact Match Accuracy (%). Horizontal axis: Total Number of Data Points c. Legend: Incontext-only (ATLAS) / RAG-only (ATLAS) / Incontext-only (RAVEN) / RAG-only (RAVEN).

content.title: RAG is in-context optimization
content.content:
RAG is in-context optimization
• Prior theory: ICL ≈ gradient descent on in-context examples
• In the linear setting, RAG also equals one gradient-descent step
• Not a claim that LLMs literally run gradient descent
Source: Li et al. (2026) [15]. Figure from Li et al. (2026) [15], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure labels: RAG / Trained FT / Partial diff / Procs diff / Partial cosine. Axes: Loss / Cosine similarity / Training steps.

content.title: RAG viewed as ICL
content.content:
RAG viewed as ICL

Aspect | Characteristics
Mechanism | Add retrieved documents to context; weights remain unchanged
Example selection | A retriever automatically selects them for each question
Weakness | Irrelevant examples can be mixed in; increasing the number can hurt
Theoretical view | Equivalent to learning on the spot using the context
Location of knowledge | Outside the weights (non-parametric knowledge)

RAG is ICL where a retriever picks the examples
Source: Ram et al. (2023) [13], Guo et al. (2025) [14], Li et al. (2026) [15]. Row 4: result in the linear setting

content.title: Chapter 3: From RAG to harnesses
content.content:
Chapter 3
From RAG to harnesses
Tool use / ReAct / context engineering / harness

content.title: Retrieval is not the only way to fetch
content.content:
Retrieval isn't the only way to fetch
• Tool use: the model calls APIs and uses results for its next prediction
• Calculator, search, translation, calendar, etc.
• Fresh values and computations also enter the input
Source: Schick et al. (2023) [16]. Figure from Schick et al. (2023) [16], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
The New England Journal of Medicine is a registered trademark of [QA("Who is the publisher of The New England Journal of Medicine?") → Massachusetts Medical Society] the MMS.
Out of 1400 participants, 400 (or [Calculator(400 / 1400) → 0.29] 29%) passed the test.
The name derives from "la tortuga", the Spanish word for [MT("tortuga") → turtle] turtle.
The Brown Act is California’s law [WikiSearch("Brown Act") → The Ralph M. Brown Act is an act of the California State Legislature that guarantees the public’s right to attend and participate in meetings of local legislative bodies.] that requires legislative bodies, like city councils, to hold their meetings open to the public.

content.title: The model decides what to fetch
content.content:
The model decides what to fetch
• ReAct: interleave reasoning & actions; feed observations back
• This loop is the basic agent form (Lecture 3)
Source: Yao et al. (2023) [17]. Figure from Yao et al. (2023) [17], Figure 1 (top row excerpt)

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
(1) Hotspot QA
Question: Aside from the Apple Remote, what other device can control the program Apple Remote was originally designed to interact with?
(1a) Standard: Answer: iPod [marked incorrect]
(1b) CoT (Reason Only): Thought: Let’s think step by step. Apple Remote was originally designed to interact with Apple TV. Apple TV can be controlled by iPhone, iPad, and iPod Touch. So the answer is iPhone, iPad, and iPod Touch. Answer: iPhone, iPad, iPod Touch [marked incorrect]
(1c) Act-Only: Act 1: Search[Apple Remote]. Obs 1: The Apple Remote is a remote control … Act 2: Search[Front Row]. Obs 2: Could not find [Front Row]. Similar: … Act 3: Search[Front Row (software)]. Obs 3: Front Row is a discontinued media center software … Act 4: Finish[yes] [marked incorrect]
(1d) ReAct (Reason + Act): Thought 1: I need to search Apple Remote and find the program it was originally designed to interact with. Act 1: Search[Apple Remote]. Obs 1: The Apple Remote is a remote control introduced in October 2005 by Apple … originally designed to control the Front Row media center program …
Thought 2: Apple Remote was originally designed to control the Front Row media center program. I need to search Front Row next and find what other device can control it. Act 2: Search[Front Row]. Obs 2: Could not find [Front Row]. Similar: ['Front Row Seat to Earth', 'Front Row Motorsports', 'Front Row (software)', …]
Thought 3: Front Row is not found. I need to search Front Row (software). Act 3: Search[Front Row (software)]. Obs 3: Front Row is a discontinued media center software …
Thought 4: Front Row (software) is controlled by an Apple Remote or the keyboard function keys. So the answer is keyboard function keys. Act 4: Finish[keyboard function keys] [marked correct]

content.title: We supply more than knowledge
content.content:
We supply more than knowledge
• Instructions, history, memory, tools, retrieved docs: one input
• Select, format, and concatenate components into one input
• This assembly is called context engineering
Source: Mei et al. (2025) [4], Anthropic (2025a) [6]. Figure from Mei et al. (2025) [4], Figure 3

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Context Engineering: Long-Term Memory / Available Tools / User Prompt / Retrieved Information.
Foundational Components → Context Retrieval and Generation: Prompt Engineering and Context Generation / External Knowledge Retrieval / Dynamic Context Assembly.
Context Processing: Long Sequence Processing / Self-Refinement and Adaptation / Relational and Structured Information Integration.
Context Management: Fundamental Constraints / Memory Hierarchies and Storage Architectures / Context Compression.

content.title: Harness: everything but the model
content.content:
Harness: everything but the model
• All 11 coding agents fit the diagram below
• Memory & Context allocates the input; LLM Integration assembles it
Source: Barbaste et al. (2026) [18], Watanabe (2026) [1]. Figure from Barbaste et al. (2026) [18], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Architecture labels: Harness / TUI / IDE / SDK / server / Agent / sub-agents / protocols / hooks / skills / plugins / MCP.

content.title: Harnesses can be seen as ICL too
content.content:
Harnesses can be seen as ICL too
Every component reaches the model as a string. Weights unchanged

Component | Form in the string | Role in ICL
System prompt | Text at the beginning | Instructions
Tool definitions | Embedded as JSON | Instructions
History and tool results | Concatenated with control-token separators | Examples and clues
Current request | Final message | Question to solve

How should huge inputs be handled?
Source: Hugging Face (2026) [19], Anthropic (2026a) [20], Yao et al. (2023) [17], Mei et al. (2025) [4]. Accessed 2026/11/6. ICL mapping is this lecture's interpretation

content.title: Chapter 4: Limits of context
content.content:
Chapter 4
Limits of context
Context window / example order / Lost in the Middle / many-shot ICL

content.title: Fitting in is different from being used
content.content:
Fitting in ≠ being used
• LLMs can now take long contexts as input
• Finding one string in long text: perfect score
• But tracking related strings or counting frequencies drops sharply with length
• Of 17 models claiming 32K+, only half held up at 32K
Source: Hsieh et al. (2024) [21]. Figure from Hsieh et al. (2024) [21], Figure 3

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: Yi34B - VT. Vertical axis: Accuracy. Horizontal axis: Sequence Length (4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K, 200K, 256K). Legend: chain=1, hop=4 / chain=1, hop=6 / chain=1, hop=10.

content.title: Example order also changes accuracy
content.content:
Example order also changes accuracy
• Experiment: classify movie reviews as positive/negative; reorder 4 examples
• Same 4 examples: order alone spans best to chance level
• Gap shrinks with size but persists in the largest model
• The best order differs by model
Source: Lu et al. (2022) [22]. Figure from Lu et al. (2022) [22], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure axes: SST-2 Accuracy (%) / Model Parameters (Billion).

content.title: Order still matters in new models
content.content:
Order still matters in new models
• Experiment: compare 15 models on 8 tasks, including news classification and arithmetic word problems
• Order matters as much as example selection, even in GPT-5 Nano
• The best ordering differs by data and task
Source: Li et al. (2025) [23], Chen et al. (2025) [24]. Figure from Li et al. (2025) [23], Figure 2

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Grouped Standard Deviation: Ordering — Avg grouped std 0.01970; Selection — Avg grouped std 0.02251.

content.title: Information position changes accuracy
content.content:
Information position changes accuracy
• High if key info is at the start or end, lower in the middle (Lost in the Middle)
• In the middle, it can fall below giving no documents
• Even untrained Qwen2 shows the U-shape: caused by causal masking and residual connections; the dip persists after pre-training
Source: Liu et al. (2023) [25], Chowdhury (2026) [26]. Figure from Liu et al. (2023) [25], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: 20 Total Retrieved Documents (~4K tokens). Horizontal axis: Position of Document with the Answer. Vertical axis: Accuracy. Legend: gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 / gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 (closed-book).

content.title: Order sensitivity depends on the model
content.content:
Order sensitivity depends on the model
• Experiment: answer with 5–100 BM25-retrieved documents in the input
• Bars: score gap, highly relevant docs placed at end vs. start
• Llama 70B: small gap. Llama 8B and Mistral 12B: large gap
• Size alone doesn't decide it. Measure on your model
Source: Gabín et al. (2026) [27]. Figure from Gabín et al. (2026) [27], Figure 9a

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure legend: bm25 + gemma3:4b / bm25 + gemma3:27b / bm25 + llama3.1:8b / bm25 + llama3.1:70b / bm25 + mistral-nemo:12b / oracle_bm25 + llama3.1:8b. Axes: Context Size / Δ F1 (reverse-standard) / Best F1 (standard or reverse).

content.title: Position improved; volume still degrades
content.content:
Position improved; volume still degrades
• Newer models: position effect nearly gone in simple search
• More items degrade all models: ~50% accuracy at 20,000 items
Source: Esmi et al. (2026) [28], McKinnon (2025) [29]. Figure from Esmi et al. (2026) [28], Figure 5

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figures by model: Grok 4 / GPT-4 / Gemini 2.5 / GPT-5. Horizontal axis: Number of Tweets. Vertical axis: Accuracy / Precision.

content.title: More examples: more accuracy, more cost
content.content:
More examples: more accuracy, more cost
• many-shot ICL: hundreds to thousands of examples boost many tasks
• Can override pre-training biases, sometimes rivaling fine-tuning
• Inference cost scales with the number of examples
Source: Agarwal et al. (2024) [30]. Figure from Agarwal et al. (2024) [30], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Bar chart: Few-Shot ICL / Many-Shot ICL. Vertical axis: Task Performance in %. Task examples: Summarization, Planning (Logistics), Problem-solving (MATH), Classification, Code Verifier, Big-Bench Hard.

content.title: Unused text costs the same per token
content.content:
Unused text costs the same per token

Approach | Included in every input
Model knowledge only | Question
Full-text input | Question + all the materials
Pass via retrieval | Question + top-ranked chunks
Fetch via tools | Question + tool descriptions + fetched results

Input cost = tokens × unit price × requests
Source: Anthropic (2025a) [6], Ji (2025) [7]. Table reworked from original slide 23

content.title: Measure to decide both volume and order
content.content:
Measure to decide both volume and order

Aspect | Research findings
Input length | Simple search can be solved; tracking and aggregation deteriorate sharply as length increases
Example order | Ordering matters as much as example selection
Information position | Accuracy drops in the middle; newer models improve this
Effect of ordering | Varies with model and data; no universal ordering works for everything
Number of examples | More examples raise accuracy, but cost also increases proportionally

Measure to decide how much context, and in what order
Source: Hsieh et al. (2024) [21], Lu et al. (2022) [22], Li et al. (2025) [23], Liu et al. (2023) [25], Esmi et al. (2026) [28], Gabín et al. (2026) [27], Agarwal et al. (2024) [30]

content.title: Chapter 5: Context is everything
content.content:
Chapter 5
Context is everything
Knowledge conflicts / Irrelevant context / Poisoning / Prompt injection

content.title: Context failures fall into four types
content.content:
Context failures fall into four types

Type | What happens
Poisoning | An error enters context and compounds in later decisions
Distraction | Long history pulls the model toward repeating past actions
Confusion | Unnecessary tools or documents induce irrelevant choices
Clash | New information contradicts old information and leads reasoning astray

Source: Breunig (2025) [31]. Type names and descriptions are from Breunig's article; the original Japanese translations are by this lecture

content.title: Language bias sways citations
content.content:
Language bias sways citations
• Experiment: relevant and irrelevant docs in different languages
• Relevant docs in English: accurate citations; else, accuracy drops
• Models may favor a document's language over its relevance
Source: Ki et al. (2025) [32]. Figure from Ki et al. (2025) [32], Figure 5

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Models compared: LLaMA-3.1 8B / LLaMA-3.3 70B / Qwen-3 14B / Gemma-3 27B. Legend: tgt (rel.), En (irrel.) / En (rel.), tgt (irrel.). Language labels: ar, bn, es, fr, ko, ru, sw, zh.

content.title: Outdated documents override right answers
content.content:
Outdated docs override right answers
• Experiment: add one outdated doc to questions solved without retrieval
• That alone flips 30% of Llama's and 37% of Qwen's answers to wrong
• Dates alone are not enough; stating how long info is valid helps
Source: Ahmed et al. (2026) [33], Ouyang et al. (2025) [34]. Figure from Ahmed et al. (2026) [33], Figure 2

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure headings: Models lag on recent reversals / Stronger directives increase poisoning.

content.title: Contradictions make answers inconsistent
content.content:
Contradictions make answers inconsistent
• 3 kinds of knowledge conflict: context–context, context– memory, intra-memory
• The model picks one side arbitrarily; answers are inconsistent
• Add dates and versions; specify which takes priority
Source: Xu et al. (2024) [35]. Figure from Xu et al. (2024) [35], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Question: Which team has won the most FIFA World Cup championships?
I. Contextual Knowledge (Context): Retrieved Documents / User Prompt / Dialogue. Inter-context conflict / Context-memory conflict.
Example sentences: Brazil holds the record for the most FIFA World Cup wins. / Germany has officially claimed the title of the most successful national team... / With a staggering total of five World Cup triumphs, the Brazilian... / I think Argentina has won the most championships.
II. Parametric Knowledge (Memory): Intra-memory conflict.
Italy is the most successful national team in the history of the World Cup, having won four titles (1934, 1938, 1982, 2006).
As of my last update in April 2023, the national team with the most FIFA World Cup championships is Brazil. They have won the tournament a total of five times.

content.title: Whether context wins depends on the model and setting
content.content:
Context wins? Depends on model & setting
• In rule reasoning, larger models suppress prior knowledge less
• With the same rule written as code, larger models comply more
• Safety training can be overridden by example sequences; robustness varies by model
Source: Xu, M. et al. (2026) [36], Polyakov & Kuznetsov (2026) [37], Dai & Patel (2026) [38]. Figure from Xu, M. et al. (2026) [36], Figure 2

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: Logic Zone (Reasoning) / Inertia Zone (Intuition). Axes: Logit Difference / Model Size. Prompt Type: Natural Language / Code Grounding. Models: Pythia (Base) / Llama (Instruct) / Qwen (Instruct).

content.title: Garbled documents reduce correct answers
content.content:
Garbled docs cut correct answers
• Experiment: OCR PDFs into text, count correct RAG answers
• Both character errors and broken tables/formatting reduce correct answers
• Performance drops especially on questions about tables, formulas and figures
Source: Zhang et al. (2025) [39]. Figure from Zhang et al. (2025) [39], Figure 5

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: Qwen2-7B / Qwen2-72B. Legend: Incorrect OCR and RAG Error / Correct OCR but RAG Error / Incorrect OCR but Right Answer / Correct OCR and Right Answer.

content.title: Irrelevant context lowers accuracy
content.content:
Irrelevant context lowers accuracy
• Adding one irrelevant sentence sharply lowers accuracy
• An “ignore it” instruction partly recovers it
• Leave out irrelevant text, or mark it as irrelevant
Source: Shi et al. (2023) [40]. Figure from Shi et al. (2023) [40], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Original Problem: Jeanne wants to ride the Ferris wheel, the roller coaster, and the bumper cars. The Ferris wheel costs 5 tickets, the roller coaster costs 4 tickets and the bumper cars cost 4 tickets. Jeanne has 5 tickets. [Irrelevant Sentence] How many more tickets should Jeanne buy?
Options for the Irrelevant Sentence Topic: In-Topic [ROLE] rides [NUMBER] kilometers to the bus station every day. Off-Topic The shoe size of [ROLE] is [NUMBER].
Options for [ROLE]: Lexical Overlap with Original Characters? Jeanne’s father, Jeanne’s sister, Jeanne’s neighbor... / Ada, Jack, Mary, Tom...
Options for [NUMBER]: In-Range / Out-of-Range / 100, 1000, 5000...

content.title: Retrieved text is not instructions
content.content:
Retrieved text is not instructions
• Models don't distinguish who wrote what
• They follow commands embedded in retrieved documents (indirect prompt injection)
• Separate data and instructions in how the input is built
Source: Greshake et al. (2023) [41]. Figure from Greshake et al. (2023) [41], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure text: Prompts / Inputs / Hello! / How may I "help" you? / Adversary-steered output.

content.title: Models do not vet their data
content.content:
Models don't vet their data

Input property | Effect on output found in research
Bias | Favors English documents and misses relevant documents in other languages
Freshness | Follows outdated documents and turns previously correct answers into errors
Contradiction | Chooses one side without justification; answers are inconsistent
Structure | Broken tables or formatting reduce correct answers
Provenance | Follows commands embedded in documents

Input properties become output properties
Source: Ki et al. (2025) [32], Ahmed et al. (2026) [33], Xu et al. (2024) [35], Zhang et al. (2025) [39], Greshake et al. (2023) [41]

content.title: Chapter 6: Testing know-how by experiment
content.content:
Chapter 6
Testing know-how by experiment
Harness engineering / AGENTS.md / Compaction / Subagents / Verification

content.title: Context engineering
content.content:
Context engineering
• Definition: a set of strategies for selecting and maintaining all the tokens that enter the input at inference time
• Write a prompt once; re-curate context every turn (Curation)
Source: Anthropic (2025a) [6]. Figure from Anthropic (2025a) [6]

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Prompt engineering vs. context engineering
Prompt engineering for single turn queries: Context window → System prompt / User message → Assistant message
Context engineering for agents: Possible context to give model → Curation → Context window → Assistant message / Tool call → Tool result → Message history
Possible context: Doc / Tool / Memory file / Comprehensive instructions / Domain knowledge / Message history
Context window: System prompt / Doc 1 / Doc 2 / Memory file / Tool 1 / Tool 2 / User message / Message history

content.title: Practice: from inputs to mechanisms
content.content:
Practice: from inputs to mechanisms

Target | Practical know-how (2025–2026)
Rules | Keep AGENTS.md a minimal table of contents
Tool descriptions | Explicitly write out implicit assumptions and refine the descriptions
Retrieval | Load only the needed parts, when needed
Compaction | First preserve without omissions, then trim
Memory | Write progress and decisions to external notes
Subagents | Separate exploration and receive only summaries
Verification | Build it in as a mechanism rather than merely requesting it in instructions

Source: Anthropic (2025a) [6], Anthropic (2025b) [42], Hashimoto (2026) [43], Lopopolo (2026) [8], Trivedy (2026) [44], Anthropic (2026b) [45], Böckeler (2026) [46]

content.title: Rules as a minimal table of contents
content.content:
Rules as a minimal index
• System prompts: aim between too specific and too vague
• AGENTS.md is an index, not an encyclopedia: only the essentials
Source: Anthropic (2025a) [6], Lopopolo (2026) [8], Hashimoto (2026) [43]. Figure from Anthropic (2025a) [6]

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: Calibrating the system prompt. Comparison: Too specific / Just right / Too vague.

content.title: Experiment: context files
content.content:
Experiment: context files

Item | Experimental design
Experiment | Gloaguen et al. (2026)
Task | Fixing issues in real repositories (SWE-bench Lite and others)
Held fixed | Task, agent and model
Varied | Context file: none / LLM-generated / developer-written
Models | 4 models, including Sonnet-4.5 and GPT-5.2
Measured | Task success rate, number of steps and inference cost

Only the context file in the input is varied
Source: Gloaguen et al. (2026) [47]

content.title: Context files do not change success rate
content.content:
Context files don't change success rate
• Figure: x-axis = 4 models; bar color = context file condition
• Result: success rate unchanged for all 4 models; inference cost up 20%+
• Verdict: conditional. Helps for non-standard conventions
Source: Gloaguen et al. (2026) [47], Khatri (2026) [48]. Figure from Gloaguen et al. (2026) [47], Figure 3

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Model comparison chart: SONNET-4.5 / GPT-5.2 / GPT-5.1 MINI / QWEN3-30B. Vertical axis: Success Rate.

content.title: Refine tool descriptions
content.content:
Refine tool descriptions
Anthropic (2025b) “Writing effective tools for agents”
• Descriptions and specs enter the input and steer tool calls
• Spell out implicit assumptions, as if briefing a new colleague
• Define inputs/outputs clearly; avoid ambiguity. Measure with evals Tool definitions are model input too
Source: Anthropic (2025b) [42], Anthropic (2025a) [6]

content.title: Experiment: richer descriptions
content.content:
Experiment: richer descriptions

Item | Experimental design
Experiment | Hasan et al. (2026)
Task | MCP-Universe (finance, maps, browser operation and others)
Held fixed | Tool implementation and task
Varied | Tool descriptions: original / augmented by an LLM
Models | GPT-4.1, Qwen3-Coder and GLM-4.5
Measured | Success rate, partial completion and number of steps

Only the tool descriptions in the input are varied
Source: Hasan et al. (2026) [49]

content.title: Descriptions alone change results
content.content:
Descriptions alone change results
• Figure: original vs. augmented description of the same stock-price tool
• Result: the median increase in success rate is 5.85 percentage points; steps increase by 67%
• Verdict: conditional. Worse in 17% of cases; short descriptions sometimes suffice
Source: Hasan et al. (2026) [49], Wang, P. et al. (2026) [50]. Figure from Hasan et al. (2026) [49], Figure 2

content.title: Fetch it when needed
content.content:
Fetch it when needed
Anthropic (2025a) Just-in-time context retrieval
• Don't preload all relevant data; keep only references like file paths
• Load needed parts with tools at runtime (just-in-time retrieval)
• Exploring is slower than pre-fetching; both can be combined Put in the input only what the current task needs
Source: Anthropic (2025a) [6]

content.title: Experiment: amount of code
content.content:
Experiment: code amount

Item | Experimental design
Experiment | Sam-Bodden (2026)
Task | 70 multi-file fixes from SWE-bench Verified
Held fixed | The location to fix (provided as ground truth) and model
Varied | How code is presented: full files / skeleton / needed parts only
Model | Claude Sonnet 4.6 (temperature 0)
Measured | Resolution rate (judged by tests) and token count

Only the amount and form of code in the input is varied
Source: Sam-Bodden (2026) [51]

content.title: Only the needed parts suffice
content.content:
Only the needed parts suffice
• Figure: left = resolution rates for 3 conditions; right = tokens per resolved task
• Result: full files solve 19 tasks and needed parts solve 25 (no statistically significant difference); the token count is 1/5
• Verdict: supported. However, missing evidence is more harmful than extra code
Source: Sam-Bodden (2026) [51], Zhang, S. et al. (2026) [52]. Figure from Sam-Bodden (2026) [51], Figure 4

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: Resolve, N=70 (pre-registered) / Cost of a resolve.
Condition | Resolved | Tokens
full files | 19/70 | 94K tokens
structured tiers | 23/70 | 26K tokens
keep/drop | 25/70 | 19K tokens
Axes: resolve rate (Wilson 95% CI) / context tokens per resolve (thousands).

content.title: Compaction: preserve first
content.content:
Compaction: keep first
Anthropic (2025a) Techniques for long-horizon tasks
• Summarize a conversation near the limit; start a new window with it
• Prioritize keeping everything first, then trim the excess
• Lightest step: clear old tool calls and results Over-trimming loses details that matter later
Source: Anthropic (2025a) [6], Anthropic (2026b) [45]

content.title: Experiment: rewriting the playbook
content.content:
Experiment: rewriting the playbook

Item | Experimental design
Experiment | Zhang, Q. et al. (2025): a record of one case
Task | AppWorld (complete tasks by operating applications)
Held fixed | Model weights (no training)
Varied | The playbook in the input; the LLM rewrites the entire playbook each time
Baseline | Accuracy without the playbook
Measured | Playbook token count and accuracy after each update

Weights unchanged; only the playbook in the input is updated
Source: Zhang, Q. et al. (2025) [53]

content.title: Rewriting collapses the context
content.content:
Rewriting collapses the context
• Figure: x-axis = playbook updates; y-axis = playbook tokens
• Result: a single rewrite collapses 18,282 tokens to 122, and accuracy falls below the no-context baseline
• Verdict: supported. Over-trimming loses details needed later
Source: Zhang, Q. et al. (2025) [53]. Figure from Zhang, Q. et al. (2025) [53], Figure 2

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: # tokens in context / # adaptation steps. # Tokens: 18,282, Accuracy: 66.7 → # Tokens: 122, Accuracy: 57.1. Accuracy w/o context: 63.7.

content.title: Experiment: varying context length
content.content:
Experiment: varying context length

Item | Experimental design
Experiment | Xue (2026)
Task | Code audit following a Skill with 24 mandatory items
Held fixed | Skill and audit task
Varied | Surrounding context: 11,000 / 300,000 characters (relevant / irrelevant)
Model | Codex (gpt-5.4-mini), 10 runs per condition
Measured | Number of runs satisfying all 24 items (pass)

Only the context around the Skill is varied
Source: Xue (2026) [54]

content.title: Long context causes rules to be missed
content.content:
Long context drops rules
• Table: top 3 rows = context lengths; bottom 2 = with fixes
• Result: passes fell from 8 to 3 of 10; a few required items get skipped
• Verdict: leaving context untrimmed can also cause harm. Supplement mandatory requirements with external checks

Condition | Passes
Short context (11,000 characters) | 8/10
Long, relevant context (300,000 characters) | 3/10
Long, irrelevant context (300,000 characters) | 3/10
+ Generic self-check | 5/10
+ External checklist | 10/10

Source: Xue (2026) [54]. Table built from results in Xue (2026) [54]

content.title: Memory: write to notes
content.content:
Memory: write to notes
Anthropic (2025a) Structured note-taking
• Regularly save progress and decisions to notes outside the window
• After context is cleared, read notes back and continue
• Examples: ToDo list, NOTES.md, progress file Memory is an external record to feed back into the input later
Source: Anthropic (2025a) [6], Ji (2025) [7]

content.title: Experiment: tracking value updates
content.content:
Experiment: value updates

Item | Experimental design
Experiment | Fan, X. et al. (2026)
Task | Answer with the current value after conversations spanning multiple sessions
Held fixed | Conversations (234 scenarios in which values change partway through)
Varied | How history is provided: memory / retrieval / full history
Models | Qwen-3.5-9B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and others
Measured | Whether the answer is the current value, an outdated value or another error

Only how history enters the input is varied
Source: Fan, X. et al. (2026) [55]

content.title: Updated values are not tracked
content.content:
Updated values aren't tracked
• Figure: left = recall of stored facts; right = tracking updated values
• Result: ≤30% correct, with memory or full history
• Verdict: conditional. When a stored value is later updated, the old one is used
Source: Fan, X. et al. (2026) [55], Peng (2026) [56]. Figure from Fan, X. et al. (2026) [55], Figure 1

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Long Horizon Fact Recall ≠ Long Horizon State Tracking
A. Recall capability: I got a cat. / How old is he? / He’s just a kitten, only 3 months old! / several sessions / I’d like to buy my cat a collar for his adoption anniversary. It should have his initials on it. / {cat = Smokey} / Ordering one collar with initial “S.” Happy birthday Smokey! / PASS: the retrieved fact is still directly useful.
B. State-tracking capability: 1600 annotations, 5 annotators, budget $600 total → several sessions → changed to 1200 annotations → several sessions → What’s the current budget? → retrieve("budget") → {budget = $600} → The current budget has $600 left. / STATE DRIFT: retrieved a stale fact and treated it as current.

content.title: Separate context with subagents
content.content:
Separate context with subagents
Anthropic (2025a) Subagent architecture
• Give each a focused task in a clean context window
• Return the results of exploration spanning tens of thousands of tokens as a 1,000–2,000-token summary
• Exploration details stay out of the main agent's context Only the summary reaches the main agent's input
Source: Anthropic (2025a) [6], Anthropic (2026b) [45]

content.title: Experiment: context passed to subagents
content.content:
Experiment: subagent context

Item | Experimental design
Experiment | Hu & Ramachandran (2026)
Task | Reasoning problems and question answering that derive an answer from evidence
Held fixed | Task and base evidence (sufficient on their own to solve it)
Varied | Context passed to the child agent: none / selected conclusions / all conclusions, including outdated ones
Models | Qwen3 from 0.6B to 14B (5 sizes)
Measured | Accuracy (difference from providing no additional context)

Only the context in the subagent's input is varied
Source: Hu & Ramachandran (2026) [57]

content.title: Carrying over old context hurts
content.content:
Carrying over old context hurts
• Figure: x = no. of old conclusions; y = gap between passing all and passing none
• Result: passing everything makes mid-size models worse than passing nothing
• Verdict: supported. Selective passing beats passing everything
Source: Hu & Ramachandran (2026) [57], Ding et al. (2026) [58]. Figure from Hu & Ramachandran (2026) [57], Figure 2

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: Inheritance harm vs dose (synthetic core). Horizontal axis: stale dose d (conflicting inherited conclusions), 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. model: 0.6B / 1.7B / 4B / 8B / 14B.

content.title: Build verification into the system
content.content:
Build verification into the system
A common claim in 2026 harness engineering
• Agents grade their own work leniently. Use a separate evaluator
• Add a mechanism that triggers checks before finishing
• Use post-hoc sensors (tests, linters, reviews) Don't “ask” for verification: “build it in”
Source: Anthropic (2026b) [45], Trivedy (2026) [44], Böckeler (2026) [46]

content.title: Experiment: stronger verification instructions
content.content:
Experiment: stronger check prompts

Item | Experimental design
Experiment | Wiedmann et al. (2026)
Task | 4 scientific tasks (astronomy, genomics and RNA)
Held fixed | Task and other agent settings
Varied | Strength of verification instructions (4 levels) and presence or absence of a verification tool
Models | Qwen3.5-122B and Step-3.7-Flash
Measured | Proportion of runs that actually checked the answer

Instructions manipulate the input; a verification tool is a mechanism outside the input
Source: Wiedmann et al. (2026) [59]

content.title: Instructions alone do not change behavior
content.content:
Instructions alone don't change behavior
• Figure: blue = actual verification; the 4 groups show instruction strength, and the right-hand entry in each group has a tool
• Result: stronger instructions leave behavior almost unchanged; providing a tool roughly triples actual verification
• Verdict: supported. Writing in the input can't reach everything
Source: Wiedmann et al. (2026) [59], Treude & Baltes (2026) [60]. Figure from Wiedmann et al. (2026) [59], Figure 4

[Supplementary transcription of figure/image text]
Figure: Share of Occurrences / Verification Levels. Conditions: Baseline / Oracle / Asked / Reported / Binding. Legend: No Verification / Format-Only Verification / Interim Verification / Reference-Based Verification.

content.title: Measure practical know-how, too
content.content:
Measure practical know-how, too

Verdict | Practical know-how examined in this chapter
Supported | Retrieval when needed / compaction that preserves first / selectively passed context / verification built in as a mechanism
Conditional | Minimal rules / refining tool descriptions / writing to memory
Common point | Adding input increases cost; effects vary with the task and conditions

Use the experimental methods to test it yourself
Source: Anthropic (2025a) [6], Anthropic (2026b) [45], Liu & Han (2026) [61]

content.title: Summary
content.content:
Summary
• Ch. 1: Rarer facts are harder to answer. Adding knowledge through further training of the weights is difficult
• Ch. 2: ICL learns from the input without changing weights. RAG is ICL in which a retriever selects the examples
• Ch. 3: Intent, situation and procedures are also supplied through the input. Harnesses can also be viewed as ICL
• Ch. 4: In the input ≠ used. Measure to decide amount and order
• Ch. 5: Input properties carry into output. Models don't vet data
• Ch. 6: Know-how is a hypothesis too; test it like these experiments

```python
def chat(first_question: str) -> None:
    client = genai.Client(api_key=get_api_key())
    session = client.chats.create(model=MODEL)  # the SDK's Chat holds the history
    question = first_question
    while question:
        response = session.send_message(question)  # sends history so far + this question
        print(response.text)
        usage = response.usage_metadata
        print(f"[tokens] input {usage.prompt_token_count} / output {usage.candidates_token_count}")
        question = input("\n[Next question (blank line to quit)] ").strip()
```

INSTRUCTIONS = """\
You are a learning support agent for the AI Engineering Pilot Course (AIE2026).
- Always check the glossary with search_glossary before answering about terms or course-specific information.
- Use get_lecture_summary when asked about the content of a session.

    """

(b) Pi: what is in its prompt, and what isn't
